doc.title: DeFranco Buddy — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Later life, Terry Gibbs and Artie Shaw
title: Tommy Dorsey's harsh and generous sides
summary: A new Miller recruit quit; Dorsey fired a joking trumpeter but paid DeFranco's hospital bills.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money

blocks.x: Right, you talked about the one kid who came on the bus for one night, with the Glen Miller Orchestra and didn’t even make it to the.

Didn’t even make it to the first job. No, he was in Connecticut somewhere, New England some place and his family brought him to the club that we were playing, the place that we were playing, and he sat it. It was kind of an audition, and he was a fine player and I said, “You have the job.” And he went back and packed his bag and he got on the bus with the guitar and bags and we traveled all night to New York. Of course, the animals in the group got a hold of him, and that happens, too, you know. The new comer on the bus, its sort of initiation. And we got into…
Drinking, right? They made him drink, drink, drink.
Yeah, a little. Yeah, they got him drunk, kind of, I guess, sick. We got to the hotel and he got off the bus and he said to me, “I can’t do this.” And he never played the first night, he went home.
Imagine how he would have felt in Tommy Dorsey’s organization.

Oh, boy. Well, Tommy Dorsey, somebody, we were in a train one time, a young fellow that played, a young fellow I think he was a trumpet player. Tommy was telling jokes, and when Tommy told a joke it was on cue, everybody would laugh on cue, naturally. He’d tell a joke and everybody, “Yeah!” And this stupid kid decided to tell a joke. “I have one.” And Tommy says, “Oh, you do, huh?” Ok, and he told this joke and he stammered and it flopped, it was terrible, nobody laughed. And Tommy said, “Ha-ha-
ha, very funny. Tell you what you do. Get your stuff together and get off at the next station, you’re through.”
A mother never wants to hear a story like that.

Oh, no, no. But that was the nasty side of Tommy, but he had both sides. You know, I got sick in Florida one time, went into the hospital with a bad throat and a lot of problems. And he sent his doctor from New York to take care of me. And after a week in the hospital I never saw a doctor’s bill or a hospital bill, and I got paid. So that was the other side of Tommy Dorsey.
